children: Business activity in the eurozone and India picked up in September, according to surveys released Wednesday, a sign that key parts of the global economy remain resilient in the face of high energy prices.
The global economy slowed only slightly in the second quarter, weathering the jump in energy costs triggered by the conflict between the U.S. and Iran.

That stronger-than-expected momentum appears to have been maintained in the third quarter, despite a fresh increase in energy prices as the conflict nears its seventh month without a resolution in sight, coupled with a jump in borrowing costs as yields on government bonds rise.

S&P said its Purchasing Managers Index for the eurozone--which measures activity in the services and manufacturing sectors--rose to 53.1 in September from 52.0 in August to reach its highest level in almost three-and-a-half years.
A reading below 50.0 points to a contraction, while a reading above that threshold points to an increase in activity. Economists had expected the surveys to record a slowdown.

"Manufacturing, spearheaded by Germany, is enjoying its best growth spell for over four years, spurred by rising AI and defense spending, but service sector growth is also perking up to signal a broad-based improvement in the economic growth story," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

The eurozone economy grew 0.6% in the second quarter, having stagnated in the first three months of the year. Williamson said the PMI readings for the three months of the third quarter point to a growth of 0.4%.

New orders expanded at the fastest pace since May 2022, an indication that growth is likely to be sustained over coming months. Businesses also reported a slight increase in payrolls for the second straight month.
So surprising has the eurozone's recent economic strength been that some economists viewed the results of the surveys with some skepticism.

"A eurozone economy that remains completely unharmed by an energy price shock and supply chain disruptions is a welcome surprise," wrote ING Bank's Carsten Brzeski in a note to clients. "Let's hope it doesn't turn out to be a mirage.
The surveys also recorded a pickup in the costs faced by businesses, and the prices they in turn charged their customers rising at a faster pace.

Combined with fresh signs of robust growth, signs of stronger inflationary pressures increase the likelihood that the European Central Bank will again raise its key interest rate before the end of this year, having lifted borrowing costs in June and earlier this month.

The surveys also pointed to an unexpected revival in France, with its PMI recording the first increase in activity for 10 months and the strongest in more than two years. That pickup reduces the risk of a slide into recession for Europe's weakest economy, which contracted in the second quarter after stalling in the first.

By contrast, activity in the U.K. slowed in September, although costs and prices charged also rose at a faster pace. The Bank of England has not followed the ECB and more recently the Federal Reserve in raising its key interest rate, and signs of weakness in economic output may keep it on a separate path.
Similar surveys pointed to an acceleration in Indian business activity, and a slight slowdown in Australia.
